D1:
Two problems. (1) Priority: Core is the lowest AnimationPriority. The default Animate script's idle/walk tracks run at Idle/Movement, which are higher, so they win the blend on the arm joints and your swing barely shows. Set the priority to Action (or Action2-4): re-export it from the Animation Editor, or set track.Priority = Enum.AnimationPriority.Action before Play. (2) Humanoid:LoadAnimation is deprecated. Load through the Animator, once, outside the click handler, so you don't create a new track on every click:
```lua
local char = player.Character or player.CharacterAdded:Wait()
local animator = char:WaitForChild("Humanoid"):WaitForChild("Animator")
local track = animator:LoadAnimation(script.SwingAnim)
track.Priority = Enum.AnimationPriority.Action
tool.Activated:Connect(function()
    if not track.IsPlaying then track:Play(0.05) end
end)
```
Also make sure the animation is owned by the game's owner (user or group), or it won't load in live servers.
D2:
Problem 1: the camera is client-side. Each client has its own CurrentCamera, so setting it from a server Script changes nothing the player sees. Problem 2: in the LocalScript, CameraType is still Custom, so the default PlayerModule camera script rewrites Camera.CFrame every frame and snaps it back behind the character. Fix: in a LocalScript, wait for the camera, set cam.CameraType = Enum.CameraType.Scriptable, then set the CFrame (or tween it with TweenService). When the cutscene ends, set CameraType back to Custom and CameraSubject back to the Humanoid.
```lua
local cam = workspace.CurrentCamera
cam.CameraType = Enum.CameraType.Scriptable
cam.CFrame = workspace:WaitForChild("CutsceneCam").CFrame
-- ...later
cam.CameraType = Enum.CameraType.Custom
```
If StreamingEnabled is on, WaitForChild the CutsceneCam part (or make it persistent). To start the cutscene from the server, fire a RemoteEvent to the client.
D3: CanvasSize is a fixed 600 px, so once the item list is taller than 600 px the extra items fall outside the canvas and can't be reached by scrolling. Hand-computing the size from item count also breaks with padding, screen scaling and UIScale. Cleanest fix: set ScrollingFrame.AutomaticCanvasSize = Enum.AutomaticSize.Y and CanvasSize = UDim2.new(0, 0, 0, 0), so the canvas grows with the UIListLayout content. Alternative: update CanvasSize from UIListLayout.AbsoluteContentSize in GetPropertyChangedSignal("AbsoluteContentSize") (CanvasSize = UDim2.fromOffset(0, size.Y + padding)). Also set ScrollingDirection = Y. Don't give the item buttons scale-based Y sizes, because a scale Y is relative to the canvas and the sizes start feeding back on each other.
D4: 1) Too weak: a 20x2x20 part (800 studs^3) has a mass of about 560 (plastic density 0.7), and with workspace.Gravity 196.2 its weight is roughly 110,000 force units. 5000 is about 5% of that, so it never lifts. Compute the force: part:GetMass() * workspace.Gravity (sum the mass of the whole assembly) plus whatever extra lift you want. 2) Off-centre attachment: a force applied at a corner creates torque, so the platform tips. 3) RelativeTo defaults to Attachment0, so the force is in the attachment's local frame. Once the part tilts, 'up' tilts with it and the force pushes sideways, so it slides and spins away. Correct setup: put the Attachment at the centre of mass (CFrame at the origin), set VectorForce.RelativeTo = Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo.World, set Force = Vector3.new(0, mass * workspace.Gravity, 0) (or set ApplyAtCenterOfMass = true), and add an AlignOrientation (or a damping/PD controller) to keep it level. For hovering at a set height, use AlignPosition or a PD controller on the height error with damping. A constant force on its own will accelerate it forever or let it drift.

```lua
local function attachPet(pet: BasePart, player: Player)
    local hrp = (player.Character or player.CharacterAdded:Wait()):WaitForChild("HumanoidRootPart")
    pet.Anchored = false
    pet.CanCollide = false
    pet.Massless = true
    local a0 = Instance.new("Attachment"); a0.Parent = pet
    local a1 = Instance.new("Attachment"); a1.CFrame = CFrame.new(0, 2, 3); a1.Parent = hrp -- behind (+Z) and above
    local ap = Instance.new("AlignPosition")
    ap.Attachment0, ap.Attachment1 = a0, a1
    ap.Responsiveness = 25; ap.MaxForce = math.huge
    ap.Parent = pet
    local ao = Instance.new("AlignOrientation")
    ao.Attachment0, ao.Attachment1 = a0, a1
    ao.Responsiveness = 25; ao.MaxTorque = math.huge
    ao.Parent = pet
    pet:SetNetworkOwner(player) -- smooth for the owner; cosmetic only
end
```
Key rules: use AlignPosition plus AlignOrientation (the modern movers) with two attachments, and put the target attachment on the HRP with the offset (the HRP's +Z is behind it). Set CanCollide = false and Massless = true so the pet doesn't push the player or drag them around. Tune Responsiveness/MaxForce rather than using RigidityEnabled, which teleport-snaps. Give the player network ownership for smoothness (or keep it on the server) and never trust anything about the pet. Re-attach on CharacterAdded, clean up when the player leaves, and set CanQuery/CanTouch to false.
D7:
```lua
local PathfindingService = game:GetService("PathfindingService")
local path = PathfindingService:CreatePath({
    AgentRadius = 2, AgentHeight = 5, AgentCanJump = true,
    Costs = { Lava = math.huge, Water = 20 },
})
local function moveTo(humanoid: Humanoid, root: BasePart, target: Vector3)
    local ok = pcall(path.ComputeAsync, path, root.Position, target)
    if not ok or path.Status ~= Enum.PathStatus.Success then return false end
    local blocked = path.Blocked:Connect(function() end)
    for _, wp in path:GetWaypoints() do
        if wp.Action == Enum.PathWaypointAction.Jump then humanoid.Jump = true end
        humanoid:MoveTo(wp.Position)
        if not humanoid.MoveToFinished:Wait() then break end
    end
    blocked:Disconnect()
    return true
end
```
Key rules: Costs keys match the PathfindingModifier Label ("Lava") and terrain material names ("Water"). math.huge makes a region impassable; a finite cost like 20 only discourages it, so water is still used when there's no reasonable dry route. Wrap ComputeAsync in pcall and check path.Status. Jump on PathWaypointAction.Jump with AgentCanJump = true. MoveToFinished times out after 8 seconds, so call MoveTo per waypoint. On path.Blocked, recompute. Call root:SetNetworkOwner(nil) so the server controls the NPC.

```lua
local DataStoreService = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local winsStore = DataStoreService:GetOrderedDataStore("Wins")

local function refresh()
    local ok, pages = pcall(winsStore.GetSortedAsync, winsStore, false, 10)
    if not ok then warn(pages) return end
    for rank, entry in pages:GetCurrentPage() do
        local userId = tonumber(entry.key)
        local okName, name = pcall(Players.GetNameFromUserIdAsync, Players, userId)
        updateRow(rank, okName and name or ("User " .. userId), entry.value)
    end
end
while true do refresh(); task.wait(60) end
```
Key rules: GetSortedAsync(false, 10) returns highest first, and only the first page is needed. Ordered store values must be positive integers. Keys are tostring(UserId), never names. Wrap every call in pcall. Refresh about once a minute, not per frame, to stay within DataStore budgets (check GetRequestBudgetForRequestType). Cache UserId-to-name lookups. Write wins with UpdateAsync/IncrementAsync when a win happens (or on save), and keep the main save in a regular DataStore; the ordered store is only an index. Results are eventually consistent.

```lua
-- (a) non-spatial looping music (LocalScript or server; plays for everyone)
local music = Instance.new("AudioPlayer")
music.Asset = "rbxassetid://MUSIC_ID"; music.Looping = true; music.Volume = 0.5
music.Parent = workspace
local out = Instance.new("AudioDeviceOutput"); out.Parent = music
local w1 = Instance.new("Wire"); w1.SourceInstance = music; w1.TargetInstance = out; w1.Parent = music
music:Play()

-- (b) spatial campfire
local fire = workspace.Campfire
local crackle = Instance.new("AudioPlayer")
crackle.Asset = "rbxassetid://CRACKLE_ID"; crackle.Looping = true; crackle.Parent = fire
local emitter = Instance.new("AudioEmitter"); emitter.Parent = fire
emitter:SetDistanceAttenuation({[0] = 1, [40] = 0.5, [90] = 0})
local w2 = Instance.new("Wire"); w2.SourceInstance = crackle; w2.TargetInstance = emitter; w2.Parent = fire
crackle:Play()
```
Key rules: nothing plays unless it's wired. For non-spatial sound, wire AudioPlayer to AudioDeviceOutput. For spatial sound, wire AudioPlayer to an AudioEmitter on a part or attachment. Players hear the emitter through an AudioListener (by default on the camera via SoundService.DefaultListenerLocation; if you build custom routing, add an AudioListener on the camera or character and wire it to an AudioDeviceOutput). Emitter and listener need matching AudioInteractionGroup. Falloff comes from the SetDistanceAttenuation curve (up to 400 points). AudioPlayer.Volume defaults to 1, whereas Sound defaults to 0.5. A looping player never fires Ended. Check Wire.Connected when debugging.

```lua
local MarketplaceService = game:GetService("MarketplaceService")
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local SUB_ID = "EXP-1234567890"

    if subId == SUB_ID then refresh(player) end

    while true do task.wait(900)
        for _, p in Players:GetPlayers() do task.spawn(refresh, p) end
    end
end)
```
Key rules: check on the server only. Subscription ids are strings. Check on join, on UserSubscriptionStatusChanged, and periodically (about every 15 minutes). The perk is live state: compute it from IsSubscribed each time and never save it permanently to DataStore. Don't grant on PromptSubscriptionPurchaseFinished; wait for the status check. Revoke when IsSubscribed becomes false, but not when a check errors. Apply the 2x multiplier in server coin code and add the chat tag via TextChatService OnIncomingMessage/ChatWindowConfiguration based on the attribute. Any one-off monthly bundle should be tied to a paid cycle (GetUserSubscriptionPaymentHistoryAsync), not to IsSubscribed.
D11: Cars: give the driver network ownership of the whole vehicle assembly (VehicleSeat does this automatically when a player sits; or call SetNetworkOwner(driver) on the root part on the server after Seated). The client simulates the physics, so steering has no round-trip lag. Set it back to the server (SetNetworkOwner(nil) or automatic) when the driver leaves. Security: the owning client controls that assembly's physics, so an exploiter can teleport or fling their car. The server must sanity-check it on Heartbeat (speed and position deltas against a cap, no-clip/teleport distance) and correct or kick. Don't let car collisions apply authoritative damage to others without server checks. NPC guards: call SetNetworkOwner(nil) on every guard's parts (after they're parented and unanchored) so the server always owns them. Otherwise, automatic ownership hands them to nearby players, which causes the flinging: an exploiter who owns the guard's physics can move or fling it. Pathfinding, damage and AI live on the server. Exploiters can still fling server-owned parts by ramming them with their own owned character or car, so limit that with CollisionGroups, by capping guard velocity, and with anti-fling checks. In 2026, Workspace AuthorityMode = Server (Server Authority) makes the server authoritative with client prediction, as an alternative for competitive games.
D12: The engine keeps versions: every write to a standard DataStore key makes a version, and superseded versions are kept for 30 days (the vault says roughly the first write per UTC hour is kept as a restore point; Unverified). APIs: DataStore:GetVersionAtTimeAsync(key, timestampMs) returns the version that was current at the moment just before the bad update (the simplest option). ListVersionsAsync(key, Enum.SortDirection.Descending, minDateMs, maxDateMs, pageSize) lets you browse versions in a window. GetVersionAsync(key, version) reads a specific one. RemoveVersionAsync deletes a version if needed. Tool design: an admin-only command or Open Cloud script takes a UserId and the update time, fetches that version, and shows a diff for the admin to confirm. Write it back with UpdateAsync (bumping a save version/flag), only while the player is offline or their session is locked; otherwise their next autosave overwrites the restore. Log every restore. Creator Hub's Data Stores Manager and Open Cloud data-store endpoints can also list and restore versions. Limits: 30 days only. Point-in-time accuracy depends on which versions were kept (hourly granularity), so the snapshot may be slightly older or miss very recent progress. These calls cost DataStore request budget. It works per key, so data spread across several keys needs each one restored. Ordered DataStores have no versioning.
D13: Use Open Cloud with an API key on your web backend (never in the browser). (1) Announcements: the backend calls the Open Cloud MessagingService endpoint (POST .../universes/{universeId}:publishMessage, topic "Announcements", message of 1 KB or less). Each server subscribes once with MessagingService:SubscribeAsync("Announcements") and shows it to its players. Delivery is best-effort and typically takes 1-2 s, so also store the latest announcement in a DataStore/MemoryStore for servers that start later. (2) Item grant: don't write directly into a live player's save, because the server's autosave would clobber it. Write the grant to a pending-grants queue keyed by UserId (an Open Cloud DataStore entry, or a MemoryStore that is cleaned up), with a unique grantId. Then publish a MessagingService nudge {userId}. The server holding that player (or the next server they join, which checks pending grants on PlayerAdded) claims the grant with UpdateAsync, applies it to the session data, marks the grantId as processed (idempotent), and saves. Security: one API key per tool with minimal scopes (messaging publish plus that datastore) and an IP allowlist, admin auth and audit logging on the panel, and handle 429s with retry-after. Open Cloud shares the experience's DataStore budget.
D14: Bindable (and Remote) events serialize arguments by deep copy: tables arrive as new tables and metatables are stripped, so invObject arrives as a plain table with no methods (inv:Add() errors with "attempt to call a nil value"). Functions aren't passed, keys may change (mixed/non-string keys are dropped or converted), and identity is lost. Mutations on the receiver don't affect the sender's copy, so state goes out of sync. Instances like the Player pass by reference. ModuleScripts: require returns the same cached table to every Script in the same VM/context, so put the inventory service in a ModuleScript (InventoryService.get(player) returns the actual object with its metatable). Other scripts call methods directly, share one source of truth, get typed APIs, and need no serialization. The usual design is a single Script entry point (bootstrap) that requires service modules, with Signal-style module events instead of BindableEvents for internal communication. Keep BindableEvents only for loose fire-and-forget notifications that pass plain data or Instances.
D15: UnreliableRemoteEvent is right for high-frequency, ephemeral and superseding data like aim direction, cosmetic positions and footstep VFX, where a lost or late packet doesn't matter because a newer one comes soon. It doesn't take up the reliable ordered queue, so hits and purchases on normal RemoteEvents stop waiting behind it. Constraints: delivery isn't guaranteed and there's no ordering, so include a timestamp or sequence and ignore stale packets. The payload must be 1,000 bytes or less or it is silently dropped; send compact values (e.g. a quantised yaw/pitch or a buffer), not big tables. Messages over the throttle are dropped rather than delayed, and messages are dropped if there's no connected handler. Never use it for state changes, damage, currency or purchases (keep those on reliable RemoteEvents with server validation). Still validate and rate-limit on the server. Also reduce the volume: send aim at about 10-20 Hz only when it changes, batch several players into one broadcast, let clients play footstep VFX locally from replicated character movement instead of networking them, and don't re-broadcast the event to the client that sent it.
D16: MessagingService limits (Roblox docs): message size is 1 KB, so a ~3 KB payload fails outright. Received messages per topic are 40 + 80 x servers per minute (about 40,040/min at 500 servers), but this design produces 500 servers x 12 publishes/min = 6,000 publishes/min, each fanned out to 500 subscribers, which is 3,000,000 deliveries/min. That's far past the per-topic and the experience-wide receive limit (400 + 200 x servers per minute, about 100,400). Sends per server are 600 + 240 x players per minute, so the send side is OK, but receiving is the bottleneck, and every server must also parse 500 messages every 5 s. Behaviour: delivery is best-effort, typically 1-2 s, with no guaranteed delivery or ordering and no persistence, so a new server sees nothing until the next round and lost messages leave gaps. Throttled messages are dropped. Better: have each server write its summary to a MemoryStore (a SortedMap with an expiry of about 30 s, keyed by JobId) every 10-30 s, and let lobby servers read the list with paging. Keep listings tiny (JobId, count, a few fields) and use MessagingService only for small nudges.
D17: Limits: HttpService allows 500 requests per minute per game server across all HttpService calls; going over makes requests fail (with about 30 s stalls). Three per join plus one per kill on a busy server can hit that, and the external API may also rate-limit (429). HttpEnabled must be on, and requests only run from servers (Studio requests come from your machine). Fix: queue analytics events and flush them in batches (e.g. one POST with an array every 30-60 s or at N events), wrap calls in pcall, retry with exponential backoff and respect retry-after on 429, and drop or aggregate low-value events (e.g. count kills instead of sending each one). Consider Roblox's AnalyticsService for in-engine analytics. API key: never hard-code it. Anyone with edit access, any leaked place file and every script copy exposes it, and you'd have to rotate it. Store it in Creator Hub Secrets and read it with HttpService:GetSecret("name"), which returns a Secret that can be added into headers (it can't be printed as plain text). Use one minimal-scope key per purpose with IP/universe restrictions. Open Cloud endpoints also have per-key and per-API rate limits, and Open Cloud DataStore calls share the experience's DataStore budget.
D18: Camera: client camera updates should run in RenderStepped, or better RunService:BindToRenderStep("FollowCam", Enum.RenderPriority.Camera.Value + 1, fn). They run just before the frame renders, after input, so the camera matches the frame drawn. Heartbeat runs after physics and isn't synced to rendering, so the camera lags behind the character by a frame and jitters. Use the dt and lerp with a dt-correct alpha (1 - exp(-k*dt)). For a custom camera, set CameraType to Scriptable (or bind after the default camera's priority). Server projectile: RenderStepped and BindToRenderStep exist only on the client (there's no rendering on the server), which is why it errors. Use Heartbeat (after physics; frame dt) for movement/raycast stepping, or PreSimulation/Stepped if you're setting physics-related values before the simulation step. Use the dt argument, never a fixed per-frame amount. In 2026 with fixed simulation/Server Authority, use RunService:BindToSimulation for deterministic movement. Better still, simulate the projectile with raycasts on the server at Heartbeat and let clients render the visuals locally.
D19: Use the Input Action System (IAS) for a new 2026 game. ContextActionService still works but is client-only and legacy-style. IAS also runs on the server and is required by Server Authority. Structure (instances, which can be built in Studio): InputContext (a group of actions you enable/disable and prioritise, e.g. "Gameplay" and "Menu") > InputAction (e.g. Sprint as Type Bool, Interact as Bool; Direction1D/2D/3D or ViewportPosition for analog input; read with GetState() or the Pressed/Released/StateChanged events) > InputBinding children (KeyCode such as LeftShift, ButtonL3 or ButtonX, with modifiers; touch via UI button bindings). Bind every action for keyboard, gamepad and touch. To block gameplay input in menus, disable the InputContext; don't use require(PlayerModule):GetControls(). Default player scripts: the PlayerModule control/camera scripts are moving onto IAS through Workspace.PlayerScriptsUseInputActionSystem. It's been opt-in since June 2026, is planned to be on by default in early 2027, and the property and old script path are planned for removal around mid 2027. Opt in now so you don't need to migrate later.
D20: Turn it on in Workspace by setting AuthorityMode = Server (the Server Authority section; full release July 9 2026). It forces NextGenerationReplication, Workspace.PlayerScriptsUseInputActionSystem, SignalBehavior = Deferred, StreamingEnabled and UseFixedSimulation. What it does: the server owns and runs the authoritative simulation, including characters, so clients can no longer move themselves arbitrarily via network ownership, and invalid movement is rejected. Clients predict locally and resimulate (roll back and replay) when the server disagrees, so input still feels responsive. Script changes: move simulation and gameplay logic into RunService:BindToSimulation callbacks (a fixed step), and keep it deterministic (use time(), not os.clock or tick). Read input through InputAction (the Input Action System), not UserInputService/ContextActionService. Keep predicted state in attributes (the first 64, with names and strings of 50 characters or less). Guard side effects such as VFX and sounds with RunService:IsResimulating() so they don't double-fire after mispredictions. Don't Destroy, reparent or EquipTool inside bound functions. Read the server view of the camera with Player:GetCameraState(). Make the code work with deferred signals and streaming (WaitForChild, no immediate-fire assumptions). Old SetNetworkOwner-based setups don't carry over.
D21: Use Workspace.UseFixedSimulation together with RunService:BindToSimulation(callback, frequency, priority). With fixed simulation enabled, the bound callback runs at a fixed rate (default Enum frequency Hz30, priority 2000) regardless of render FPS, with a constant dt, so a 30 FPS client, a 144 FPS client and the server step identically. Requirements: Workspace.UseFixedSimulation must be enabled (Server Authority forces it on). Movement code must be deterministic: use the provided fixed dt and time(), not os.clock or per-frame dt, with no randomness unless seeded. Guard side effects such as VFX, sounds and remotes with RunService:IsResimulating(), because under Server Authority callbacks may re-run during rollback. Don't destroy or reparent instances inside the callback. Read input from the Input Action System. Without fixed simulation, the fallback is your own fixed-timestep accumulator in PreSimulation. Note: under fixed simulation, Motor6D Transform writes may not apply while an animation is playing (forum-reported, unverified).
D22: As of 2026, Lighting.Technology is deprecated and locked to RobloxScriptSecurity, so game scripts can't read or write it (hence the error) and it's hidden from the Properties panel. It's replaced by two properties: Lighting.LightingStyle (Enum.LightingStyle.Realistic, the default, or Soft) and Lighting.PrioritizeLightingQuality (bool, default true). The vault gives an approximate mapping (unverified): Future becomes Realistic + true, ShadowMap becomes Soft + true, and Voxel becomes Soft + false; Legacy, Compatibility and Unified are deprecated. Lighting style is a design choice set in Studio, and lighting quality now scales automatically with the device and the player's graphics settings. A client settings menu shouldn't toggle the engine technology; instead let the player's graphics quality handle it, or adjust client-side visuals (shadows on parts, post-effects, Atmosphere) locally. Check the result on both phone and PC.
D23:
Yes. Instance:QueryDescendants takes a CSS-like selector that filters by class, tag and attribute in one engine call:
```lua
local coins = workspace:QueryDescendants("BasePart.Coin[$Collected = false]")
for _, coin in coins do
    -- ...
end
```
Selector grammar: ClassName, .Tag, #Name, [$Attribute = value], > (child), >> (descendant), :has(), :not(). It's a one-shot snapshot. For a live set, use CollectionService:CreateCollection("BasePart.Coin[$Collected = false]") and assign OnAdded/OnRemoved. The vault doesn't confirm that the BasePart class selector matches subclasses (Part, MeshPart), so test it; you can drop the class and use ".Coin[$Collected = false]" with an IsA check. The older alternative is CollectionService:GetTagged("Coin") plus a GetAttribute filter, which is still far cheaper than GetDescendants every round.
D24: All four have built-ins: lerp(a, b, t) becomes math.lerp(a, b, t). The remap function becomes math.map(x, inMin, inMax, outMin, outMax) (it doesn't clamp; clamp yourself if needed). The x ~= x check becomes math.isnan(x) (math.isinf and math.isfinite were also added; never compare against math.nan). Manual bit shifting into a buffer becomes buffer.writebits(b, bitOffset, bitCount, value) and buffer.readbits(b, bitOffset, bitCount), with offsets in bits, bitCount 0-32 and unsigned results, so the 3-bit and 5-bit fields pack directly. Out-of-range access throws and buffers don't grow automatically. (bit32.extract/replace also still exist for integer-level packing.)
